concept.name: Harami
concept.definition: A two-candlestick pattern in which a small real body is completely contained within the prior session's large real body (the reverse of an engulfing pattern); 'harami' is Japanese for 'pregnant'. Read generically, it marks a sudden loss of momentum in the prevailing trend and is treated in technical analysis as a potential reversal warning, directional (bullish or bearish) according to the trend it interrupts.
concept.intuition: After a big, confident candle, the market suddenly shrinks to a small candle that fits entirely inside the prior body, as if the trend caught its breath and participants hesitated.
concept.mechanics: From OHLC data: candle 1 has a large real body; candle 2's open and close both fall strictly inside candle 1's open-close range. Bullish harami: large black body then small body after a decline. Bearish harami: large white body then small body after an advance. If candle 2 is a doji, the pattern is a harami cross.
concept.formula: Harami when min(O2, C2) > min(O1, C1) and max(O2, C2) < max(O1, C1), with body 1 large relative to recent candles.
concept.failure_modes: Harami are frequent and low-powered: many are followed by trend continuation, making them one of the weaker reversal families without confirmation. In tight ranges they occur constantly and mean little.
concept.misconceptions: A harami compares real bodies, not full ranges; a small candle inside the prior candle's full high-low range but not inside its body is an inside bar, a related but distinct concept. It is also a warning of stalling momentum, not a confirmed reversal.
concept.example: In an uptrend, a stock prints a long white candle (50.00 to 53.00), then a small candle that opens at 52.20 and closes at 51.80, entirely inside the prior body. The harami warns that upside momentum has stalled pending the next candle's direction.
